title: What kitchen does a private chef need? A practical checklist
summary: Check whether your kitchen suits a private chef dinner, including cooking facilities, fridge space, equipment and serving arrangements.Focus keyphrase: private chef kitchen requirements
body_markdown:
You don’t need to guess whether your kitchen is suitable for a private chef. Send photographs and describe the facilities before you book. The chef can check the menu against the space and tell you what needs to change.


The important question is whether your kitchen suits the particular meal and group size. A setup that works for six people may be difficult for twenty, especially if you want several courses served at once.


## **Show the cooking facilities**


Photograph the oven, hob and available worktop. Say how many ovens you have, whether the hob is induction and whether any appliance has a fault. If the chef asks about an unfamiliar appliance, send its model details.


Don’t rely on estate-agent photographs that hide the working parts of the room. Current images are more useful, especially in a rented property where the equipment may have changed.


The most useful briefs on yhangry describe the kitchen in a line or two: “one oven and an induction hob”, “a four-oven AGA with an induction hob” or “a small modern galley kitchen, but a large living area”. That is usually enough for a chef to judge which menus will work, and what to leave out. When one host asked for pizza at a 40th birthday, Chef Pete M, who has completed more than 100 yhangry bookings since November 2025, said in his proposal that he wouldn’t include it unless the property had a proper pizza oven, and worked those flavours into other dishes instead.


## **Make room for ingredients and preparation**


Ask how much fridge space the chef needs and keep it free. A fridge already packed with drinks can leave nowhere for food that needs to stay chilled. Agree where drinks can go so they don’t get in the way of the chef’s food storage.


Clear the worktops and explain where guests will gather. If the kitchen is also the main social space, agree which area needs to stay free for preparation and movement. Some hosts like guests to watch the chef at work, and[Chef Eduard’s case study on cooking live in front of guests](https://yhangry.com/private-chef-live-cooking-dinner-party-eduard-yhangry/) shows how that can become part of the evening. Plan how children and pets will be kept safely away from hot equipment and busy service.


## **Count equipment and tableware**


Check pans, roasting trays, chopping boards and other equipment against the chef’s requirements. Do the same for plates, bowls, cutlery, glasses and serving dishes. A multi-course menu may need more items than a single-course meal for the same group.


Ask what the chef brings and what you supply, because arrangements vary. Chef Nicola H, who has also completed more than 100 yhangry bookings in that time, tells hosts in her proposals: “I usually use the house’s crockery but bring everything I need to prepare the dishes.” If you’re short of anything, say so in your request. If something must be hired, agree who arranges it, what it costs and how it will be delivered. Don’t leave that conversation until the chef is loading their car.


## **Think beyond the kitchen**


The route to the dining table matters. Stairs, narrow doorways or a long walk can affect service and staffing. Tell the chef if the meal will be served in a garden room, a separate building or an upstairs room. If you definitely want waiting staff, mention it in your request and ask the chef to include it in their quote.


Confirm parking, unloading access and any lift restrictions. If you live in a managed building, check the rules for supplier access and arrange any permissions in advance.


## **What if the kitchen is small?**


A small kitchen can still support the right menu. Ask the chef which formats work and where preparation can happen. They may suggest different dishes, fewer last-minute components or extra equipment, but feasibility needs to be agreed for your actual venue. Some chefs also do much of the preparation in their own kitchen beforehand: Chef Alastair S explains on his yhangry profile that he preps a lot at home so he isn’t in your kitchen all day getting in the way. Chef Jessica, whose[plating we covered in a case study](https://yhangry.com/plating-tips-chef-jessica-yhangry/) , says she enjoys the challenge of cooking in different kitchens. Her large, colourful sharing plates work just as well where the facilities are basic. She brings her own lightweight metal platters and wooden boards, and makes fresh pasta at home rather than bringing the machine. Her advice to other chefs: expect that “the client’s plates are smaller than you practised, or their oven is hotter”, and adapt.

It works for bigger groups too: in September 2025,[Chef Fouad M](https://yhangry.com/booking/chef/fouad-m/) cooked canapés and a three-course dinner for 32 guests at a home wedding, and the couple said in their review they weren’t sure how he managed it in their small kitchen.[Fouad’s 500+ events](https://yhangry.com/private-chef-income-chef-fouad-yhangry/) are the subject of another of our case studies. These prices are examples from past bookings, not quotes.


## **What if there are no cooking facilities?**


Say so clearly from the start. Don’t assume a private chef can provide a full mobile kitchen, or that the venue allows one.

It can still work with the right brief. In December 2025, a company hosting a Thanksgiving dinner for 12 in its office explained that it had only a kitchenette with a sink, a small fridge and a microwave, so the food would need to arrive cooked and ready to plate.[Chef Nadine L](https://yhangry.com/booking/chef/nadine-l/) and her assistant served roast turkey, herb-crusted salmon, a full set of sides and pumpkin pie, for a total of £1,092. Nadine has completed more than 290 yhangry bookings, and[her case study](https://yhangry.com/meal-prep-chef-nadine-yhangry/) covers how she runs meal prep alongside private events.


## **Before you book**


Send the chef a short description of your kitchen, a few photographs, your guest count and your preferred menu. A few practical messages now can prevent a much bigger problem on the day. If you’re booking for a rented house, our[holiday home chef](https://yhangry.com/f/catering/holiday-home-chef/) page covers what to expect.


When you’re ready,[send yhangry your date, postcode, guest count and a line about your kitchen](https://yhangry.com/booking/quote/) , and chefs will reply with menus that fit the space.


FAQ


Do I need a big kitchen to hire a private chef?


No. Chefs on yhangry regularly cook in galley kitchens, flats with a single oven and rented cottages with limited equipment. What matters is telling the chef about the space before you book, so the menu suits it.


Will the chef use my pots, pans and plates?


It depends on the chef and the menu. Many chefs cook with the equipment in your kitchen and serve on your tableware, but some bring their own. Ask what the chef needs from you, and say in your request if you’re short of anything.


Do I need to buy the ingredients?


No. The chef’s quoted price includes the cost of ingredients unless you have explicitly asked for a quote without them. The chef does the shopping and arrives with everything at the agreed time.


Can a chef cook on an AGA or an induction hob?


Yes. Many yhangry bookings are cooked on AGAs and induction hobs. Mention what you have in your request so the chef can plan their timings and bring any pans that suit the hob.


What if my venue has no kitchen at all?


Say so in your first message. Some chefs can prepare food elsewhere and bring it ready to plate, but that is a different service from cooking on site, and the venue’s rules still apply.
